en: The *Maitreya-sūtra-yuyi* (An Exposition on the Intent of the Maitreya Sūtra) consists of ten sections:
first, the introduction to the king; second, the explanation of the title.
Third, distinguishing the essential body of the sutra;
fourth, discussing cause and effect;
fifth, the long duration of the appearance in the world.
Sixth, a discussion on the true and manifested aspects of attaining enlightenment;
seventh, a differentiation of the number of people in the three assemblies;
eighth, a discussion on attaining nirvana at the same time as Śākyamuni.
Ninth, clarifying the Great and Small Vehicles; Tenth, miscellaneous analysis and distinctions.

1. Introduction on the King. First, regarding the introduction on the King: the appearance of all Buddhas in the world is for the sake of the great causal conditions. Therefore, they abide in a state where even the initial aspiration is not yet sufficient; they exclusively awaken to the Mahāyāna of non-attainment and cultivate the myriad practices. Thus, they may ascend to Tuṣita Heaven to preach the *Prajñāpāramitā* for the sons of the gods.
Or, when fifty-six billion seven hundred million years have passed, he descends to Jambudvīpa and attains the realization of awakening.

Therefore, whether it be a former Buddha or one who subsequently achieves the Way through the eight phases, succeeds to the throne, or succeeds to the honor, all are those in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha).

Therefore, it was previously recorded that Śākyamuni first taught and subsequently entrusted [the Dharma] to Maitreya; this clarifies that this Bodhisattva’s merit is equal to the ten stages (*bhūmi*), his virtue has perfected the noble practices, and he has surpassed the "Patience of the Supreme" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) among the three patiences. Only then shall he transform this defiled land into that Pure Land, where the human lifespan is eighty-four thousand *yojanas* and a single sowing yields seven harvests. How much more so when famous flowers and soft grasses float through the air and fill the ground, when precious treasuries and divine wonders overflow the valleys and hollows, and when, during the three assemblies for preaching the Dharma, the Way encompasses devas and humans, such that all names and designations awaken to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

2. Explanation of the Title, Part Two. Regarding the title of this sutra, if it were preserved in its foreign (Hū) pronunciation, it should be called *Buddha-bañcha-anāra-maitreya-bodhisattva-anuttara-samādhi-tuṣita-deva-sūtra*. In the Han language, it means: *The Sutra on the Awakened One’s Discourse on the Great-Minded Being Maitreya’s Ascent to the Tuṣita Heaven*.
Now, to distinguish these different names:
one is called Virocana, also known as Janaka, which translates here as "Accomplished.
Buddha translates here as "The Awakened One," "The Knower," "The Seer," and so forth.
The Tripitaka Master says:
it is pure awakening (*viśuddha-bodhi*).
*Sūtra* is also called *sūtra*, *sūtra*, *sūtra*, and *sūlana*; thus there are four variant names.
The Tripitaka Master says:
*Sūtra* and *Vinaya* encompass five different names.

Here, the two sutras on the Descents from Above and Below cite both the foreign (Hu) and Chinese sounds to illustrate the two types of causes: persons and dharmas. The reason the sutra clarifies this is that practitioners are all people who have either already been born or will be born in future lives, and thus they shall attain Buddhahood.
Next, [the text] distinguishes between Ajita and Maitreya.
Ajita means "Invincible" (Wunengsheng) in this language; thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states that he is "one whom none can conquer.
As for Maitreya, he is also called Maitreya or Maitreyaka.
The *Vasumitra-sūtra* also states: “The *Upāśūnyatā-sūtra* says ‘Ara-mi-le’,” both of which refer to contemplating Maitreya.
However, according to tradition, some say that “Ajita” is his name and “Maitreya” is his clan-name (gotra);
others say that “Ajita” is his clan-name and “Maitreya” is his name.
The two commentators have not yet detailed their respective choices or rejections.

Both were individuals who practiced compassion in past kalpas and had long cultivated the causes of loving-kindness; they were named "Maitreya" (the Compassionate One) because they established themselves through the cultivation of compassion, and the name was used to designate the person by virtue of their excellence. Thus, he is called Maitreya.
Therefore, the *Śāstra* states: "Ānanda asked the Buddha:
'By what causes and conditions did he obtain the name Maitreya?
The Buddha replied:"
In the distant past, during the Jambudvīpa world, there appeared a Buddha named Puṣya.

At that time, there was a king named Dharmāśoka who, when he went to the Buddha’s dwelling, saw a bhikṣu entering the samādhi of loving-kindness; his body was serene and tranquil, and he emitted a great radiance.
When the King saw this, he asked the Buddha,
"In what samādhi has this bhikṣu entered, that his radiance is such as this?
The Buddha replied to the King:
This bhikṣu has entered the samādhi of loving-kindness.
Upon hearing these words, the king’s faith increased and his admiration deepened, and he said:
"This concentration of loving-kindness is so truly sublime; I too shall practice this samādhi of loving-kindness."
At that time, King Dharmaruci was none other than the present Maitreya.

Having given rise to this mind of loving-kindness toward the world, he has been constantly named Maitreya ever since; because of his long-standing cultivation of this nature, even when he attains Buddhahood, he shall still be called the Compassionate One (Maitreya).
Just as when the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was born, all his physical surroundings were like lamps; therefore, he was named Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
Regarding the original cause and condition of his begging for oil to make offerings to the bhikṣus, he was called Dīpamāla, and is also named Dīpaṅkara Buddha.
As the *Śabda-śāstra* states: "That which has feet is called a *dīpa*, while that which has no feet is called a *dīpa*.

The twelve-fascicle *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* says: "Maitreya was born in the village of Kapila in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī into the family of a minister; upon his birth, he possessed the thirty-two marks, his body was the color of purple-gold, and his countenance was exceptionally distinguished."
The regent was filled with joy and summoned a physiognomist to examine him.
Because the physiognomist’s name was Śobhita, he asked:
"What signs did this child possess at the time of his birth?"
He replied, "His mother’s natural disposition was not virtuous; however, since she conceived him, she has shown compassion and pity toward those who suffer.
The physiognomist spoke joyfully:
"This child must possess a heart of compassion.
For this reason, they established a name for him, calling him Maitreya.
His parents loved and cherished him with boundless affection; his extraordinary and sublime marks were so harmonious that his fame was proclaimed throughout the land.

The king of Vārāṇasī, named Brahmadatta, heard of this and was filled with fear; apprehensive that his own throne might be usurped, he intended to find a means to eliminate him while he was still not yet grown.
His parents, having learned of this, sent someone to escort him to his maternal uncle.
His uncle’s name was Pāpali; he led five hundred disciples and was studying the Way in a foreign land.
After his maternal uncle obtained Maitreya, he taught him the arts and learning; before he had reached the age of ten, he had mastered the scriptures.
Later, when his uncle heard that a Buddha had appeared in the world, he dispatched Maitreya and sixteen others to the Buddha’s presence, intending to pose four questions:
first, to ask about the number of marks [of a Great Man].
2. Asking about the lifespan;
3. Asking about the disciples;
4. Asking about the nature of the sutra.
After Maitreya had finished his questioning, the Tathāgata was pleased and, in response, further expounded the Dharma for their transformation.
Fifteen of those people attained the pure Dharma-eye; each rose from their seat and requested to leave the household life.
The Buddha said,
"Welcome! and his topknot fell away of its own accord.
Furthermore, he employed skillful means to preach the Dharma for them; fifteen people attained arhatship, while Maitreya had only resolved his mind [on enlightenment] seven years prior.
Later, Maitreya returned with the Buddha to the kingdom of Kapilavastu.

The Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī personally spun and wove for the Buddha a single piece of golden-threaded *kāṣāya* robe; with focused mind and accumulated contemplation, she offered it to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One did not accept it, but instead instructed that it be offered to the assembly of monks.
Following these words, it was offered to the various images.
As it was passed among the assembly of monks, there was no one who wished to take it; however, when it reached Maitreya, he immediately took hold of it.

At that time, the Buddha passed through the country of Pāṭaliputra; his body was the color of purple, yellow, and gold, and he wore a *kāṣāya* robe woven with golden threads, the inner and outer layers perfectly matching one another. As he went on almsround, he arrived at a great precipice and stood there holding his bowl.
When the people saw him, they could not look upon him enough; though all held him in deep reverence, there was no one who gave him food.

At that time, a pearl-stringer was about to take him home to provide for him, but his wife spoke in anger, saying, "He will deprive us of our share of the pearl-stringer's profits. Maitreya, however, took this master back to the community of monks.
The Sangha extensively expounded the Dharma, and the benefit of the offerings was profound:

for the sake of that person's welfare, the Buddha spoke of how Aniruddha, by giving a single woolen blanket in a past life, shall never suffer poverty throughout all his successive births; he also spoke of the future retribution of Maitreya resulting from such generosity.
3. Distinguishing the Essential Substance of the Tenets, Part Three. First, a general classification:
The *Sūtra on the Ascent to Heaven* takes the Mahāyāna as its essential substance, while the *Sūtra on the Descent to Earth* takes the Hīnayāna as its essential substance.

The *Sūtra on the Rebirth Above* fully attests to the bodhisattva practices of the six perfections and the four immeasurables, and it also fully explicates the Middle Way and the conventional; therefore, the Mahāyāna causes and effects constitute its primary tenet, as will be clarified in the ninth section below.

The *Sūtra on the Descent into the World* (*Śūramgama-samādhi-sūtra*) distinguishes only the three categories of precepts, concentration, and wisdom—the Three Piṭakas—and thus takes the Hīnayāna as its primary tenet; consequently, it teaches the Dharma in three assemblies solely to realize the four fruits of arhatship, for it speaks only of the conventional and does not clarify the Middle Way.
Question:
Since the sūtras fully elucidate the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, how can the Hīnayāna be considered the primary tenet? Answer:

Regarding the meaning of the four virtues such as permanence (*nitya*) and bliss (*sukha*), the exposition of the Small Vehicle’s (*Hīnayāna*) nirvāṇa explains these four virtues and so forth as being spoken in contrast to its destruction of impermanence (*anitya*) and other [afflictions]; it does not necessarily refer to the preaching of the four virtues—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—to the bhikṣus who had practiced the three types of cultivation.

Alternatively, it may serve to clarify the Mahāyāna in passing; thus, the *Sūtra on the Descent* states: "Then, upon this very day, he will leave the household life and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

According to the fundamental tenets of this school, dharmas are not non-scriptural; that which is manifested by form is not non-form, and that which is manifested by fragrance is not non-fragrance, and so forth. While all dharmas are invariably scriptural, we follow the teaching of Śākyamuni to take form, sound, and so on as the essence of the scripture, clarifying them as "two yet not two."
Among the fifteen aspects, three aspects constitute the attainment of the sūtra’s essence.
If one says that the essence and the thesis differ, then the True Dharma is the essence and cause and effect are the thesis.
This is fully detailed in the *Great Sūtra Commentary* (*Dajing shu*), the *Great Chapter Commentary* (*Dapin shu*), and other such works. 4.
Discourse on Cause and Effect. Fourth, the discourse on cause and effect has three parts:
first, clarifying causal practice;
Second, the discussion of the merit of the fruit;
third, the analysis of the beginning and end.
First, the elucidation of causal practice.

The explanations in the sūtras and śāstras differ; as the *Mahālaṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states: "In each and every bhūmi, one must spend hundreds of thousands of great kalpas before accomplishing the practice of that bhūmi. This does not include those of dull faculties.
If it is as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "Kātyāyanīputra said that one cultivates the practices for the fruit over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Question:

When Kātyāyanīputra presents the "half-teaching" (*ardha-dharma*) in contrast to the bodhisattva’s practice of understanding and cultivation accumulated over kalpas, what is meant by the "half-teaching" being the Hīnayāna and the "full teaching" (*pūrṇa-dharma*) being the Mahāyāna?
Answer: It is likewise difficult to discern; however, there is that which is peripheral and that which is central.
Although Kātyāyanīputra primarily elucidates the teachings of the Hīnayāna, he also peripherally elucidates the Bodhisattva practices of the full teachings of the Mahāyāna.
What is meant by "ancillary"?

As the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "One correctly understands the true meaning within the Tripiṭaka, yet this does not obstruct the [distinctions between] the Great and Small Vehicles of that treatise. Furthermore, the "Chapter on Beneficial Actions" (*Karmārthavarga*) states: "The six pāramitās, such as dāna, result in the attainment of the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Regarding the term *asaṃkhyeya*: ten tens are called a hundred; ten hundreds are called a thousand; ten thousands are called ten thousand (*myriad*); one hundred thousand is called a *koṭi*; ten million *koṭis* are called a *nayuta*; ten million *nayutas* are called a *bimba*, and a *gata*; that which exceeds a *gata* is called one *asaṃkhyeya*.

Regarding the Śākyamuni Bodhisattva’s practice from the moment he first resolved his mind [for enlightenment]: during the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he practiced through understanding and conduct (*adhimukti-caryā*), yet he did not know for himself that "I shall become a Buddha.
During the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, although he knew for himself that "I shall become a Buddha," he did not dare to speak of it; his mind was free from fear, and he possessed this knowledge.

Since the sutra states that "Maitreya’s aspiration preceded Śākyamuni’s," the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* says: "In the past, Maitreya encountered the Buddha Bhadra-prakāśa; having come forth from that Buddha's presence, he first gave rise to the bodhicitta. Therefore, the sutra states:
"Maitreya’s aspiration arose forty kalpas before Śākyamuni’s."

Furthermore, the *Mahā-upāya-kauśalya-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra* states: "Prior to the present Śākyamuni, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Mahā-Śākyamuni. At that time, while seeing those suffering within the hell of the flaming chariot, he was only then able to give rise to the Great Mind."
From the past Great Śākyamuni Buddha down to Kanakaśikhin Buddha constitutes the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
During this time, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni did not depart from his female body.
From the time of the Buddha Kanakamuni until the Buddha Dīpaṃkara is called the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa; it was at this time that he first succeeded in leaving behind his female body.
At that time, the Bodhisattva took flowers as an offering to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, spread out a deerskin garment, and strewed his hair over the mud.
At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara sat and bestowed upon him this prediction:
"In a future age, after ninety-one kalpas have passed, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni."
"From Dīpaṃkara Buddha to Vipaśyin Buddha, this is called the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa; by cultivating and perfecting the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), one becomes a Buddha.
Second, the discussion of the qualities of the fruition.

There are proximate fruits and distant fruits; as the Sūtra says: "After twelve years from the end of the kalpa, on the fifteenth day of the second month, he will return to his place of birth, cast off his life, and be reborn in the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven. This is called the proximate fruit.
There are two kinds of distant fruits:
first, attaining Buddhahood in the lower Jambudvīpa after fifty-six billion seven hundred million years, which is the proximate fruit;
second, if one practices through the accumulation of kalpas and attains Buddhahood after the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*), this is called the true fruit, which is the distant fruit.
Question:
It may be acceptable to treat this as a horizontal, superficial outline of the treatise;
however, why do you not distinguish the vertical, subtle, and correct fruits?
Answer: The true fruit is neither near nor far, neither cause nor effect; it is not distinguished as such.
However, if one wishes to forcefully clarify it, that too is permissible.
Third, the clarification of the temporal sequence from beginning to end.
As stated in such sutras as the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra*:

"There are three periods of kalpas; in each kalpa there are one thousand Buddhas: one thousand Buddhas in the past Adornment Kalpa (*Vibhūṣaṇa-kalpa*), one thousand Buddhas in the present Worthy Kalpa (*Bhadrakalpa*), and one thousand Buddhas in the future Constellation Kalpa (*Tārakā-kalpa*)."
These three thousand Buddhas shared the same superior causes in their past practices; therefore, they attained their respective fruits sequentially over the course of three *kalpas*.

Furthermore, the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa constitute a single category; among these thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, the first four have already passed, and Maitreya is now the fifth, who is destined to appear in the world and flourish.
Since there is both a prior and a subsequent stage in the supramundane, I shall now describe them in full.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Kātyāyanīputra said:

'After three asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed, at that time the Bodhisattva cultivates the karma for the thirty-two marks for one hundred kalpas; this is a matter of mastery regarding speed or slowness—slower it takes one hundred kalpas, faster it takes ninety-one kalpas.'"
Because he scattered five flowers as an offering to the Buddha, he shall become a Buddha after ninety-one kalpas.
To state it plainly, he ought to have become a Buddha upon the completion of one hundred kalpas;
however, due to his diligent practice and asceticism, he has transcended nine kalpas, leaving him with ninety-one remaining.
"If he does not transcend [this stage], he shall attain Buddhahood after Maitreya.

Therefore, it is frequently stated in the sutras that Maitreya resolved his mind for enlightenment and practiced the Path prior to Śākyamuni, yet because he did not practice with such diligence and asceticism, he will attain Buddhahood later.
Therefore, Maitreya thought to himself:
"For a thousand asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have been born in Tuṣita Heaven and preached the Dharma to deliver the devas, yet I could not for even a moment abandon my various ascetic practices."
Because Śākyamuni practiced asceticism with such diligence, he surpassed [the remaining time] by nine *kalpas* to attain Buddhahood.

Regarding the discrepancy between the statement in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* that he surpassed twelve *kalpas* upon hearing a verse from a rākṣasa, and the statement in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* that he surpassed nine *kalpas*, various masters have explained it as follows:

he surpassed twelve *antara-kalpas* (small *kalpas*) and nine *mahā-kalpas* (great *kalpas*). Since there are three types of *kalpas*, and he surpassed three of each, this results in nine [surpassed] *kalpas*.
Question:
Why does the *Mahā-sūtra* state that the Teacher’s verse [allowed him] to transcend twelve kalpas, while the *Mahā-śāstra* names it nine kalpas? If:
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "When the Bodhisattva Xue heard the rākṣasa preach to him: 'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing.
When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss.'"
"Therefore, he transcended twelve kalpas.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The extensive explanation of the time when Puṣya Buddha appeared in the world does not definitively state that the duration of the kalpa was long."
However, that Buddha had two disciples:
one named Śākyamuni and the other named Maitreya.
Puṣya Buddha observed that while the mind of the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was not yet fully matured, the minds of the disciples he was to transform were already fully matured.
The reason for this is that Śākyamuni’s mind regards self-benefit as secondary and the transformation of others as primary;
furthermore, while Maitreya’s own mind is already fully matured, the minds of the disciples he transforms have not yet reached such maturity.
The reason for this is that practicing the path oneself is primary, while transforming others is secondary.
At that time, Puṣya Buddha thought to himself:
"The mind of a single person is easily transformed and delivered, whereas the minds of many people are difficult to subdue."
Thus, because Vipasyin Buddha wished for Śākyamuni to quickly attain Buddhahood, he entered the Great Radiance Samādhi within a jeweled cave on the Snowy Mountains.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was transforming himself into a non-Buddhist rishi to go up and gather famous flowers; there, he saw Vipasyin Buddha manifested within the jeweled cave, his body emitting radiance.

When the Bodhisattva saw the Buddha, his heart was filled with great joy. He immediately stood upon one leg, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and gazed at him with single-minded devotion, his eyes never blinking. For seven days and seven nights, he praised the Buddha in verse: "Among all that is above heaven and below heaven, none is like the Buddha;
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is likewise no peer. I have seen everything that exists within the world, And among all things, none can equal the Buddha."
"For seven nights he gazed intently at the Buddha’s eyes without once blinking; by this, he transcended nine great kalpas and attained Buddhahood within the Bhadrakalpa.
Some say: "To 'transcend' here means to transcend through the karma of the marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana); to possess the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) is called 'transcending.'"
Now I say this is not so; both the transcendent and the non-transcendent must first coexist before they can ripen.
When the activity of *prajñā* is transcendent, if one attains *prajñā*, then all things will advance.
However, during these ninety-one kalpas, the appearance of Buddhas in the world was not uniform.
As stated in the ninth fascicle of the *Śāstra*: "During the first ninety kalpas, three Buddhas appeared in the world; during the subsequent ten kalpas, one thousand Buddhas appeared."
"During the ninety kalpas, in the first kalpa there was Vipaśyin Buddha; 'Qin' (Chinese) means 'Various Views.
During the thirty-second kalpa there were two Buddhas:
the first was named Śikhin Buddha; 'Qin' means 'Fire,' and is also called 'Topknot'."
2. Vipaśyin Buddha (translated into Qin as "All-Victorious").
At the beginning of the ninety-first kalpa, there were four Buddhas:

the first was named Krakucchanda Buddha, also known as Kāśyapa Buddha; this name is not found translated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. The Tripiṭaka Master Kunlun also called him "Cap-Buddha" (*Maofo*), for when the Buddha was born, he appeared like a pearl emerging [from its casing].
The second was named Kanakamuni Buddha, which in the Qin language means "Golden Seer" or alternatively "Bent Seer";
the third was named Kāśyapa Buddha;
and the fourth was named Śākyamuni Buddha.
The four Buddhas of the Dharma-foot precede the three Buddhas of the previous [aeon], making seven Buddhas in total.
Those first three Buddhas were the Buddhas during the ninety aeons.

The lifespan of the first Buddha was eighty thousand years; the second Buddha’s lifespan was seventy thousand years; and the third Buddha’s lifespan was sixty thousand years. There are four remaining Buddhas in the ninety-first aeon, which is named Bhadra (the Auspicious).
At the beginning of the kalpa, the lifespan of humans numbered several tens of millions of years, which gradually decreased and decreased;
when it reached five hundred thousand years, a Wheel-Turning Sage King appeared to transform the world through his conduct, and from that time on, it diminished further and further.

The *Bhadra-kalpika-sūtra* states: "When the human lifespan reaches forty thousand years, the fourth Buddha of this *kalpa*, Kṣāntivādin (also known as Krakucchanda), will appear in the world during the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*), and his teaching will endure for sixty thousand years."
When the human lifespan reached thirty thousand years, the fifth Buddha, Kanakamuni, appeared in the world during the five turbidities; the sutras state that it was at forty thousand years.
When the lifespan was twenty thousand years, the sixth Buddha, Kāśyapa, appeared in the world, with a life span of twenty thousand years.

After the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the human lifespan gradually decreased until it reached one thousand two hundred years; it was at that time that Śākyamuni first ascended to Tuṣita Heaven, where he remained for four thousand celestial years, which corresponds to five billion six hundred and seventy million human years.

When the human lifespan is one hundred years, he will descend from Tuṣita to Jambudvīpa to become a Buddha; his True Dharma shall endure for five hundred years, and his Semblance Dharma for a thousand years. After fifteen hundred years have passed, the Dharma of Śākyamuni will be completely extinguished.
Another sutra states:
"In the age of the Dharma-ending period, which lasts ten thousand years,
there will be only those who practice as pratyekabuddhas."

Human life gradually becomes shortened until, at ten years of age, the three calamities arise in competition; the land falls into ruin and desolation, all evil people die out, the realm becomes sparse and empty, and whenever they see one another, they kill each other.

At that time, there appeared in the world a rishi named Guo Xiang, also known as Guo Zhi, who exhorted them, saying, "Do not kill one another. Because causes and conditions were gradually becoming more urgent and life was shortening, he urged them to cultivate wholesome deeds and the mark of compassion.
When wicked people reform their past ways and cultivate themselves for the future through the causal conditions of the sutras, the sons they subsequently bear will have a lifespan of twenty years.

As these sons in turn procreate sons, the lifespans of descendants increase to forty years, and as this lineage continues to grow, reaching one hundred years, ten thousand, thirty thousand, and sixty thousand years, a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) appears in the world to propagate his teachings. Following a succession of such kings, during the seventh period when the human lifespan reaches eighty-four thousand years, Maitreya Buddha shall appear in the world; it is at that time, when the people are peaceful and prosperous, that he descends to birth.
The *Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū-sūtra* states: "The Buddha Maitreya’s radiance shall illuminate forty *li*.
He will be born into the Brahmin caste; his father’s name is Brahmā and his mother’s name is Brahmāsūtra."
The *Mahāmaitrī-sūtra* states: "The father is the causal condition;
because he possesses the virtue of a lord of men, he is said to 'cultivate Brahma' (*brahmacarya*). This is translated as 'Good Virtue' (*śubha-guṇa*), and also as 'Good Purity' (*śubha-viśuddhi*)."
His mother’s name was Brahmavatī, which in this language means "Lord of Virtue" (德主) or also "Lord of Purity" (淨主).

The *Bhadrakalpika Sūtra* states: "The son was named Guṇabala-Bahuśruta; the attendant was named Sāgara; the disciple of wisdom was named Prajñāprabha; and the disciple of supernatural powers was named Dṛḍhavīrya."

When the Buddha was in the world, the human lifespan was eighty-four thousand years, and the True Dharma remained for eighty thousand years; his relics collectively established a great monastery to propagate the Dharma.
The Buddha Siṃha had a light that illuminated forty *li*.

He was of the noble class; his father’s name was Vīrasimha, his mother’s name was Gaṅgānirghoṣā, and his son’s name was Mahābalabahudhara. His attendant was named Sukhābhirata, his disciple of supernatural power was named Varṣa, and his disciple of wisdom was named Jñānakūṭa.
When the Buddha was in the world, the human lifespan was seventy thousand years.
He preached the Dharma in three assemblies; the True Dharma lasted for one hundred million years, and his relics spread throughout the eight directions, above, and below.
"From Krakucchanda Buddha to the ninety-ninth Buddha, they together occupied the first half of the kalpa; the latter half was used exclusively by Ruci Tathāgata.
After the parinirvāṇa of Ruci Buddha, sixty-two more kalpas passed in vain, with no Buddha appearing in the world.

After that, in the sixty-third kalpa thereafter, a Buddha named King of Pure Radiance (Vimalaprabhābhirāja) appeared in the world as a Tathāgata; his lifespan was ten small kalpas, and he transformed sentient beings.
After this Buddha has passed away, there will again be three hundred kalpas during which no Buddha shall appear.
Although there are one thousand Buddhas here, when the preceding and succeeding periods are combined, they constitute three thousand Buddhas.
Question:
Why does the Tathāgata Lohita alone employ half an eon? Answer:
It must be according to the conditions of sentient beings; it should be understood as being merely a matter of number.
Question:
For what reason are there one thousand Buddhas within this Bhadrakalpa?

Answer: The *Suvarṇabhāsottama-sūtra* states: "In the past, there was a wheel-turning monarch who appeared in the world, endowed with a full thousand sons. Each of these princes gave rise to the bodhicitta, vowing to seek buddhahood."

The father, the Holy King, wishing to admonish these thousand princes—though he had previously become a Buddha—inscribed the names of the thousand princes and, facing them, washed them with fragrant liquid, commanding the thousand kings to gather [the medicinal herbs].

The first among those reckoned as foremost was the initial Buddha; continuing in this manner down to the ninth hundredth and ninety-ninth prince, the final one prince was the thousandth Buddha by name.
The princes derided him, saying:
"When we have attained Buddhahood and completed our work of transformation, where will you dwell to deliver beings once you have become a Buddha?
Upon hearing these words, the young prince wept with grief and reflected further:
"The world is boundless and sentient beings are inexhaustible.

I now make this vow: when I become a Buddha, may the lifespan of the sentient beings in my world be equal to that of these princes, and may the number of sentient beings I deliver likewise be the same."
Thereupon, the earth shook in six ways, and the Buddha immediately bestowed upon him a prophecy.
For this reason, the last of these Buddhas alone presides over half an eon.
Because he wept and cried, he was named "The Weeper" (Rodaṇa).
Regarding the Buddha who is marked by the weeping of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, this "Weeper" is also called the "Luminous Buddha," for at the time of his birth there was a supreme radiance.
Thereupon, the princes made this vow:
"When the prince attains Buddhahood, we shall serve as his Vajra-protectors; when Loushi Buddha attains Buddhahood, we shall likewise serve as his Vajra-protectors alone."
"These are the protections of the five classes of Vajradhara.
These are the protections of the Vajrapāśa deities within the five classes. He asked:

In the Bhadrakalpa, there are one thousand Buddhas; these are indeed the thousand sons of the Universal Monarch who were prophesied by the Buddha Tiṣya. They appear in the world in succession to become Buddhas. Since there are two thousand Buddhas across the two periods of the past and future, for what reason do exactly one thousand Buddhas appear in each period?
Answer: The various Dharma masters say:
"I have not seen it stated in the sūtras that there is a causal condition."
This indeed exists, and its analogy can be stated, such as the account of the causes and conditions of the thousand Buddhas.

As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "When this Lord of Devas questioned and Subhūti answered to explain the Prajñā, it was likewise in the Buddha-fields of the Ganges-sands in the ten directions that the Lord of Devas questioned and Subhūti answered."
The reason for this is that the Way of all Buddhas is identical.

The *Dilun* and *She lun* schools, as well as the *Chengshi* and *Vibhāṣā* traditions, agree on the fundamental principle that the essence of Buddhahood is not a separate entity; rather, it is the consciousness (*vijñāna*) of sentient beings that continues without interruption until it finally achieves the ultimate fruit.
If one treats all defilements as dross, then all coarseness will be exhausted, and the realm of the wisdom of all modes will be luminous, serene, and eternally abiding.
To abide therein is to extensively cultivate the myriad practices of the multitudes, so that goodness is fulfilled and the ten thousand virtues are perfected.

Therefore, when the diamond-like mind (vajracitta) subsides, the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) immediately arises; ignorance is transformed into clarity. Thus, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The reversal of ignorance becomes clarity."
If we discuss the attainment of Buddhahood in general terms, all those who possess consciousness constitute its very substance.
Thus, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings possess a mind; all who possess a mind shall attain the threefold Bodhi."

To discuss this separately: it is only after accumulating practice over kalpas and attaining the perfection of all virtues following the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) that one is called a truly accomplished Buddha.

Now, the Mahāyāna school discusses this from a horizontal perspective and speaks of it as a provisional designation (*prajñapti*), yet it also carries this same intent. However, according to our own school’s doctrinal tenets, if other schools claim that consciousness becomes the Buddha, we say that when the mind is shattered, washed away, and purified until it is empty of provisional designations, this is called true Buddhahood.

As for Maitreya, according to the intent of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-sūtra* and the *Sarvabuddhaprasūti-sūtra*, he has long since attained Buddhahood; however, within the context of his manifest traces, he renounced the world on a single day, and thus it is on that very day that he becomes a Buddha.

If one discusses the essence of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it transcends all names, words, mind, and consciousness; it is simply the fulfillment of great compassion, never contravening its vows, and adorned with myriad virtues.

The reason it is thus is that, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, it manifests within the diverse realms; because it responds to the traces of living beings, it appears in various forms; and it does so in order to lead those beings out of existence and non-existence, as well as from birth and death.
Although their physical forms differ—just as the forms and lifespans of the seven Buddhas of the present vary—as stated in such sutras as the *Dīrgha Āgama*:
"The first was Vipaśyin Buddha, also known as Veṣṭin Buddha."
The Buddha was of the Kṣatriya royal lineage;
"Kṣatriya" here translates as "field-dividing.
His original clan name was Gautama; the Buddha’s body was two thousand four hundred li in height, with a complexion like purple-mo yellow gold, and he sat beneath the Śāla tree.
Once Lady Jin was paying homage to the Buddha; the hairpins on her head fell to the ground, yet she could not see where the gold pins had gone.
When placed horizontally, they did not reflect the Buddha’s radiance; thus one knows that the Buddha’s color is purple-molten-gold, which moreover outshines the gold of Jambūdvīpa.
Aśana in Jambudvīpa is here translated as "the age-tree.
In Southern Jambudvīpa, this tree serves as its representative name; this tree rises to a height of forty thousand *li*.

Vipaśyin Buddha’s father was named Bandhumat, his mother was named Bandhumatī, and his son was named Kṛkin. His city was named Bandhumatī, his halo extended one hundred and twenty yojanas, and his lifespan was eighty thousand years.
Second was Śikhin Buddha, also named Śi Buddha; he was likewise of the Kṣatriya royal lineage and his clan name was Kauṇḍinya.

His body was one thousand six hundred and eighty *li* in height, and his complexion was like purple-gold. A radiance of one hundred *yojanas* emanated from his entire body, and his lifespan was seventy thousand years.
The Buddha Śikhin’s father was named Mingxiang (Auspicious Signs), his mother was named Guāngyào (Radiant Splendor), and his son was named Wúliàng (Immeasurable).
Third, the Buddha Viśvabhū—also called Bìnùfù—is likewise of the Kṣatriya caste.

The lineage [of] Kauṇḍinya was one thousand two hundred and eighty *li* in height; his halo was forty *yojanas*, and the light radiating from his entire body extended for sixty *yojanas*; his lifespan was sixty thousand years.
The *Vibhāṣā* states: "The father of the Buddha was named Sudarśana; his mother was named Yaśodharā; his son was Śaikṣa; and the city was named Anupama.
The fourth, Krakucchanda Buddha—also known as Kālakocanda Buddha—was of the Brahmin caste, which here is translated as "the nature of truthful conduct."
Kāśyapa’s body was one thousand *li* tall; his halo was thirty-two *yojanas* in circumference, and his pervasive radiance extended fifty *yojanas*. His lifespan was forty thousand years.
The *Vibhāṣā* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 46, states: "The disciple of great learning was named Saṃkha.
For Po-sun Buddha (Puṣya Buddha), his father’s name was Rūpaśrī, his mother’s name was Suparṇī, his son’s name was Uttara, and the city was named Anava."
The fifth was Kanakamuni Buddha; he was also of the Brahmin caste and his family name was Kāśyapa.

His body was eight hundred *li* in height, his halo was one thousand two hundred *li*, and the light from his entire body extended for one thousand six hundred *li*. His lifespan was thirty thousand years.
He had a learned disciple named Sūdi Buddha; his father was named Nṛguṇa, his mother was named Sujayā, his son was named Mārgācārya, and the city was named Viśuddha.
Sixth is Kāśyapa Buddha, which in this language is translated as "Turtle. He was also of the Brahmin caste; "Kāśyapa" is his clan name.
His body was sixteen zhang tall, and his lifespan was twenty thousand years, though it is also said to have been thirty thousand years.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states, "Kāśyapa Buddha entered parinirvāṇa after seven days. There are differing interpretations of this meaning:
first, some say he entered parinirvāṇa after seven months;
second, others say that during the seven days he preached of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, rather than entering parinirvāṇa.
This intention seems to correspond to twenty thousand years.
The Buddha’s father was named Brahmadatta, his mother was named Vasudattā, his son was named Jayasena, the city was named Vārāṇasī, and his disciple of great learning was named Bāspa.
Seventh, Śākyamuni Buddha belongs to the Kṣatriya caste.

Śākyamuni’s body is sixteen feet tall, and his halo is seven feet in diameter. The Buddha’s lifespan was eighty years; however, there are discrepancies between this and the accounts found in the sūtras and śāstras regarding the lifespan of the Śākya clan.

The *Madhyamāgama* (Zhōngběnqǐ jīng) states, "The Buddha’s lifespan was eighty years. The two-fascicle *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "Seventy-nine [years], having reached the age of eighty. The twelfth fascicle of the *Garbhāvakrānti Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the King's Lineage" (*Wángshì pǐn*), states, "Śākyamuni’s lifespan was eighty-four years. The *Āgama Sūtras* state, "The Buddha’s lifespan was eighty-five years. The thirty-fourth fascicle of the *Śāstra* (Shìlùn) states, "The lifespan of Śākyamuni Buddha was one hundred years. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states, "A lifespan of three asaṃkhyeya kalpas is of the same kind as the lifespan of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; although it is sixteen thousand years, it is but eighty human years."
Regarding those who receive further years, because the faculties of sentient beings are capable of enduring eighty years, he enters parinirvāṇa;
as for those remaining to transform sentient beings, he entrusts them to the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and others.
In such cases, the timing differs; sometimes the intention follows what is appropriate for the object, so that one perceives that the lifespan is not fixed.
For example, the Tathāgata’s great term was eighty years, yet in his seventy-ninth year he preached the *Mahāsūtra*.

If that is so, then as for the statement in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding "more than forty years," this must refer to the account in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which further reduces the duration by one year; thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was preached during the seventy-eighth year [of the Buddha's ministry].
If that is so, taking eighty years as the fixed limit, he left home at nineteen and attained enlightenment at thirty.

Regarding the statement that he continued preaching the Dharma even when reaching the upper age limit: at the time the Buddha first preached the Dharma, there were those about eleven years old who were already able to approach the Buddha—meaning they were sufficiently mature to hear the Dharma.
By the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he had already reached sixty-one years of age.
Approximately forty years after the Buddha’s passing, when this man was one hundred and one years old, he heard the Dharma teachings in their entirety.

Regarding the teaching on the beginning and the end: as long as this person remains in the world, they will be able to expound the Dharma and transform others through their conduct; thus, the pure tradition will persist and the Buddha-dharma will flourish.
This is the intended meaning of the various masters' explanations.

The father of Śākyamuni was named King Śuddhodana, his mother Māyā, and his son Rāhula; the city was named Kapilavastu, and regarding the disciples who were preeminent in learning, it is as described in the *Gṛhapati-sūtra*.
From the time of Vipaśyin Buddha until the birth of Śākyamuni, [the Buddhas] walked seven steps and raised their hands, saying:
"All three realms are suffering; in the heavens above and the world below, I alone am the most honored."

Furthermore, they all observed from the four directions that old age, sickness, death, śramaṇas, and those practicing the Way were all heading toward the Deer Park to turn the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths; such is what the various masters have taught.
Furthermore, the seven Buddhas are all of a superior golden hue.

The eighth fascicle of the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states: "The body of Maitreya is one thousand feet tall. However, according to the *Abhisambodhi-sūtra*, it says: "His body is sixteen zhang tall, his halo extends for one hundred yojanas, and his lifespan is eighty-four thousand years."

"He is of the Brahmin caste; his father, a brahmin, is named Suddhodana (translated here as 'Pure Virtue' or 'Good Virtue'); his mother is named Māyādevī (translated here as 'Virtuous Excellence'); his son is named Rāhula (translated here as 'Virtue-Power'); the city is named Ketumatī; and his learned disciple is named Sāriputta (translated here as 'Sea-Lord')."

The second fascicle of the *Garbha-sūtra* states: "Śākyamuni was born from the side; Maitreya will be born from the crown of the head. My lifespan shall be one hundred years; Maitreya’s shall be eighty-four thousand years."
"My land is of earth, while your land is of gold;
I am in suffering, whereas you enjoy supreme bliss.

Now, Maitreya is the fifth Buddha of this Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Aeon). In the past, during the Kalpa of Adornment (Vibhūṣaṇakalpa), there were one thousand Buddhas; the first Buddha was named Padmaprabha (Flower Light) and the last Buddha was named Viśvabhū Tathāgata.
In the present Bhadrakalpa, there are one thousand Buddhas; the first Buddha is named Krakucchanda, and the last Buddha is named Roca.
In the future, in the Kalpa known as Nakṣatra, there will be one thousand Buddhas; the first Buddha is named Prabhāsa-prabha-śrī-rāja, and the last Buddha is named Sumeru-lakṣaṇa Tathāgata.

According to the *Sūtra of Praising the Three Thousand Buddhas*, it is said: "Among the thousand Buddhas of the past, the first Buddha was named Bhagavat (the Honored One Among Men), followed by Siṃhagati (Lion-Gait Buddha), and the last Buddha was named Vajrarāja (Vajra-King Buddha)."
"Among the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, the first Buddha is named Kanakavatsa, the next is Kāśyapa Muni, and the last Buddha is named Ruci.
Among the thousand Buddhas of the future, the first Buddha is named Rājarāja, and the last Buddha is named Parāvṛttacakrottama-guṇa."

5. Clarifying the Duration of the Appearance in the World. Fifth: Clarifying the Duration of the Appearance in the World. At the beginning of the kalpa, the lifespans of human beings were not uniform; some say they were thousands, tens of thousands, or hundreds of millions of years, while others say they were forty thousand years, or eighty-four thousand years.
Gradually the lifespan shortens until it reaches one hundred years, and eventually ten years; the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* is the same on this point.
Thus, the *Loutan jing* says: "When the human lifespan reaches ten years, there are three minor kalpas:
first, the kalpa of swords and blades;"
Second is the kalpa of high grain prices;
third is the kalpa of pestilence.
As for the "sword" [kalpa], it is when people are largely greedy and coarse, practicing the ten unwholesome paths of action.

If they perform good deeds, the multitude laughs at them, treating them as fools and rivals; they harbor thoughts of destruction toward one another and teach each other to commit evil, so that not a single person is virtuous.
At that time, the lifespan of the people is ten years; then, when a girl is five months pregnant, she gives birth to a child, and most people practice what is unrighteous.

The food, drink, soups, and flavors possessed by women who have married, as well as all their clothing, will completely vanish; mountains, forests, ravines, valleys, cliffs, and shores will arise spontaneously throughout the world, all the seven treasures will disappear, and there will be only thorns and brambles upon the earth.

At that time, the people did not instruct their parents nor did they honor their elders; there were no śramaṇas among them, and when people met one another, they desired only to kill each other, just as hunters see deer or gazelles and immediately wish to slaughter them.
At that time, the grasses, trees, tiles, and stones all transformed into swords and blades, and they slaughtered one another.

When the human lifespan had reached ten years, among them were those with a few marks of merit who, seeing this mutual slaughter, fled into mountains, forests, valleys, and deep rivers to hide themselves, saying:
"There is no one capable of killing me, nor shall I kill you."
"Thereupon, they lived in the mountain forests, subsisting on the roots and fruits of various trees;
their mutual killings ceased after seven days.
Furthermore, a sutra states: "The killings ceased only after seven days; those among the people who died at that time all fell into the *Niraya* hell."
Once the mutual killing had ceased, the wise emerged to meet one another and made a mutual agreement that they should not harm or kill each other.

Thereupon, the people of the world practiced virtue once more; subsequently, the children born were all twenty years of age. Later, their grandchildren lived for forty years, gradually increasing to eighty, and eventually reaching one hundred thousand, ten thousand, twenty thousand, forty thousand, and sixty thousand years.
Since they have mutually bound themselves by precepts and practiced virtuous deeds together, their lifespans will gradually increase.
Eventually, when the people of the world all reach an age of eighty-four thousand years, a Buddha shall appear in the world named Maitreya.
The rise and fall of the world follow such patterns; this constitutes the *kalpa* of weapons (*śastra-kalpa*).

As for the *kalpa* of famine (*durbhikṣa-kalpa*), people commit many unlawful evils and diseases, holding wrong views, being stingy and greedy, and out of envy they hoard wealth and do not practice charity. Rain and drought are irregular, crops fail to ripen, and grain is gradually exhausted until even a single grain of rice becomes scarce and its price skyrockets.

The husks and chaff are shed from the streets and alleys, and the leaves fall away; as the husks and leaves are exhausted, people dig beneath the earth for sustenance and eat the roots of plants and trees.
Those who were previously dead are pressed down and killed, and their flesh is eaten by others.

The more they ate, the hungrier and thirstier they became; they went to places of slaughter and even to burial grounds to gather various bones, boiling them in liquid to drink, thus sustaining themselves.
Those who die of starvation are reborn among the hungry ghosts; this is called the *jighatsā-kalpa* (era of hunger).
As for the *vyādhi-kalpa* (era of disease), all people possess right view and practice the ten wholesome paths of action, and thus they never arise within those three kalpas.

However, because people lack merit and encounter evil times and wicked people, diseases are numerous; furthermore, they have no other means of recourse and possess little virtuous karma. Thus, even if they perform many good deeds, they cannot ward off calamities, and upon encountering illness, they die immediately.

Throughout their lives, they have committed acts of plundering, burning, beating, and striking; with their minds thus deranged, at the moment of death their spirits are seized and cast directly into the three evil realms to undergo immeasurable suffering.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "If one observes the precept against killing for a single day and night, one will ultimately not be born during the kalpa of weapons or the kalpa of disease.
It further states: "If one offers *harītakī* fruit to the Saṃgha, one will ultimately not be born during the kalpa of epidemics;
if one provides a single meal as an offering to the Saṃgha, one will ultimately not be born during the kalpa of famine."
"In this Jambudvīpa, the evil kalpa may arise, whereas it is rare in other regions;
here the kalpa of swords arises, while there there is only intense anger;
here the kalpa of disease arises, while there there is only physical weakness."
This refers to the kalpa of famine, whereas that [previous one] was merely a minor drought.
These three kalpas are compiled from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Tri-dharmaka Sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, as well as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.

Regarding the "three kalpas" mentioned in the sutra, this refers to the shifting of temporal sequences where periods of evil are designated as *antarakalpa* (small kalpas); it does not mean that a distance of forty *li* constitutes what is termed the small, medium, or great kalpa.

6. Chapter Six: Distinguishing the Attainment of Enlightenment. First, we clarify the differences in the trees under which the seven Buddhas attained enlightenment, as explained according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
The first, Vipaśyin Buddha, attained enlightenment while seated beneath a Pāla tree.
The second, Śikhin Buddha, attained enlightenment while seated beneath a Puṇḍarīka tree.
The third was Viśvabhū, who attained enlightenment while seated beneath a Pāṭalī tree.
The fourth was Krakucchanda Buddha, who attained enlightenment while seated beneath a Śiṃśapā tree.
The fifth, Kanakamuni Buddha, attained enlightenment while seated beneath an udumbara tree.
The sixth, Kāśyapa Buddha, attained enlightenment while seated beneath a nyagrodha tree.
The seventh is Śākyamuni Buddha, who attained enlightenment while seated beneath a peepal tree (*pippala*).

Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā* clarifies that the names of the trees under which the first six Buddhas attained enlightenment were identical, whereas Śākyamuni alone attained enlightenment while seated beneath an aśvattha tree.
The eighth is Maitreya, who will sit beneath the Dragon-Flower Tree and attain enlightenment.
Regarding "attaining enlightenment," there are two types: true enlightenment and provisional enlightenment, as explained in the fourth section of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

Now, to clarify this: the realization of principle constitutes Buddhahood, which is precisely true Buddhahood. Second, there is the manifestation of traces that constitutes Buddhahood. Regarding the realization of principle:

from the initial cultivation of a common person up until ascending to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), one has not yet fully attained permanent abiding; it is only upon reaching the final mind through exhaustive study that the Tathāgata’s perfect clarity is realized. This is something originally non-existent that now exists; therefore, it is called the true realization of principle.

Regarding the statement that "attainment is achieved through the manifested trace": for instance, on the very day the Great Being Maitreya left the household life, he sat beneath a Dragon-Flower tree and attained equal and perfect enlightenment; therefore, it is said that attainment is achieved through the manifested trace.
In general discourse on cause and effect, there are no more than two types:

first, practicing the cause of actual cultivation to attain the fruit of actual cultivation. This refers to ordinary beings who, relying on fear, practice until reaching the stage of non-attainment and up to the tenth bhūmi; all such instances constitute the causes of actual cultivation.
After the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*), when the fruit of Buddhahood arises, this is the fruit of actual practice.

Second, regarding the fruit of attaining the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) through practicing the causes within the traces: for example, Śākyamuni’s six years of ascetic practice constitute the cultivation of causes within the traces, while his attainment of enlightenment at thirty constitutes the fruit of the response-body.
Now, Maitreya’s attainment of the Way is the response to his manifested traces. 7.

Clarifying the Differences in the Number of Those Saved in the Three Assemblies. Seventh, clarifying the differences in the number of those saved in the three assemblies, as explained according to the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*: the three assemblies of the seven Buddhas differ in the number of people they save.
First, Vipaśyin Buddha taught the Dharma in three assemblies:
at the first assembly, he delivered sixteen thousand eight hundred people;
at the second assembly, he delivered one hundred thousand people.
During the third assembly, eighty thousand people were delivered.
The second, Śikhin Buddha, also delivered people in three assemblies:
at the first assembly, one hundred thousand people were delivered; at the second assembly, eighty thousand people were delivered; and at the third assembly, seventy thousand people were delivered.
Third, Viśvabhū Buddha taught the Dharma in two assemblies to deliver sentient beings:
in the first assembly he delivered seventy thousand people, and in the second assembly he delivered sixty thousand people.
Fourth, Krakucchanda Buddha, in a single assembly, preached the Dharma and delivered forty thousand people.
Fifth, Kanakamuni Buddha, likewise in a single assembly, preached the Dharma and delivered thirty thousand people.

Seventh, Śākyamuni Buddha also preached the Dharma in a single assembly and delivered one thousand two hundred and fifty people, all of whom received the precepts by the call of "Come hither" (ehi-bhikṣu).
Various masters say:
It is unknown when this *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisūtra* was translated; as for the initial conversion of the two merchants Trapusa and Bhallika and others, no large number of people is seen there.

When he preached the Dharma for the five men, he saw only Kauṇḍinya and the other four; yet, according to the scriptures of the various devas, it is said that eighty thousand devas attained the Way, which is why it is difficult to understand.

Furthermore, it was not that these were people saved in a single assembly; rather, they were those who attained realization of the Way through different teachings heard during a single sitting, and thus came to be known as the one thousand two hundred and fifty people.
It is also said:
the three brothers, including Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and his companions, constitute one thousand, while Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, along with their followers, constitute two hundred and fifty.
It is further stated:
"The disciples of Śāriputra numbered six hundred and fifty, and those of Maudgalyāyana numbered six hundred; together they amounted to one thousand two hundred and fifty."
Regarding the statement that Śākyamuni preached the Dharma in a single assembly, this specifically refers to his teaching of the Wheel of the Four Truths within the Deer Park.
Among these seven Buddhas, there were three assemblies, one assembly, or various different assemblies.
Eighth, regarding the three assemblies at which Maitreya Buddha will preach the Dharma, the number of people saved in each differs.
As stated in the *Garbha-sūtra*, Śākyamuni addressed Maitreya in verse:
"Though you shall be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss, it shall not be as I have endured through successive hardships."
"The Dharma you preach is very easy; the Dharma I preach is very difficult.
You first preached ninety-six, then ninety-four, then ninety-two;
I first preached twelve, then thirty-six."

The three groups of people you have mentioned were those whom I previously transformed: nine hundred and sixty million who received the five precepts, nine hundred and forty million who upheld the three refuges, and nine hundred and twenty million who uttered the name "Namo Buddha" once.
"Your father, Brahmāñña, led eighty-four thousand [beings]; these were not those previously converted by me, but are the first to be delivered by you.

The *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) and this sutra likewise state that there are three types of people who were first converted by Śākyamuni; this is what is meant by the teaching of this sutra.
Furthermore, the third fascicle of the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Abiding of the Dharma" (*Dharmasthiti-parivarta*), states: "The Buddha addressed Maitreya:
'My causal conditions are now exhausted; there is no place for further instruction.'"

"The sentient beings currently to be converted shall now be divided into three parts: one part is entrusted to Ānanda to deliver; another is given to Nanda and Upāli to deliver; and the remaining part is entrusted to Maitreya to deliver and liberate."

8. Distinguishing the Simultaneous Nirvana of Maitreya and Śākyamuni from their Different Modes of Parinirvāṇa, Part Eight. Examining the Buddha, he passed away on the eighth day of the fourth month in the summer of the tenth year of King Zhou Zhuang, on the *xinmao* day; that the fixed stars ceased to appear was precisely the day of the Buddha’s birth.
The Buddha left home on the eighth day of the fourth month in the eighth year of King Hui’s reign; at that time he was nineteen years old.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the nineteenth year of King Hui’s reign, he attained enlightenment; at that time he was thirty years old.
He entered parinirvāṇa on the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifth year, at the age of eighty.

From the Buddha’s appearance in the world during the reign of King Zhuang of Zhou until the time of Qi, a total of one thousand two hundred and forty years elapsed, as is detailed in the *Great Sūtra Commentary* (*Dajing shu*).

The *Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Gathering the Dharma," states: "The Tathāgata attained enlightenment on the eighth day of the second month; on the eighth day he turned the wheel of the Dharma; on the eighth day of the second month he subdued Māra; and on the eighth day of the second month he entered nirvāṇa."
The various sūtras differ slightly in their explanations; this section clarifies the timing of Maitreya’s entry into nirvāṇa.
As the *Maitreya-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "Upāli asked the Buddha:
'World-Honored One!'"
In the past, within the Vinaya and various preceding and subsequent sūtras, it was said:
"Ajita shall attain Buddhahood.
This person possesses the body of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) and has not yet severed the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Although this person has now left the household life, they do not cultivate meditative concentration nor sever their afflictions.
The Buddha says that there is no doubt this person will attain Buddhahood.
Upon the end of his life, in which land will he be reborn?
The Buddha replied:
"This person shall pass away twelve years from now and will certainly attain rebirth in the Tuṣita Heaven, where he will extensively preach the Dharma for the sons of gods."
Upāli asked the Buddha again:
"When will this Great Being be born from Jambudvīpa into that heaven?
The Buddha replied:

Twelve years hence, on the fifteenth day of the second month, at the place of his original birth in the house of the great Brahmin Kapila in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, he will sit cross-legged and enter the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) to attain parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the people erected many jeweled stupas to make offerings to the śarīra.

Within a precious terrace on the Tuṣita Heaven, atop a maṇi palace, he was suddenly born by transformation upon a lion throne; sitting cross-legged upon a lotus flower, his body was the color of Jāmbūnada gold, sixteen yojanas in height, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics. For five hundred and sixty-seven million years, he preached the Dharma during the six periods of day and night, delivering various devaputras. Only then did he descend to be born here and become a Buddha.
Regarding the statement that one does not cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) nor sever afflictions (*kleśa*), the masters of the older commentaries say:

"This *Amitābha Sūtra* is consistent with the Dharma-wheel of the Initial Teaching (Hīnayāna), just as Śākyamuni took the example of practicing austerities for six years in the body of an ordinary person before finally attaining Buddhahood."

Since this sutra now manifests as the stage of the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*), it contains within the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* the bodhisattva practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), which constitute the practice of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). Given that these are fully discussed therein, could one say that the "provisional person" does not cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) nor sever the afflictions (*kleśa*)?
However, Upāli questioned with the mindset of the Hīnayāna.

Since the tenet of the "Half-Teaching" (Semi-Mahāyāna) holds that even a true ordinary person can attain Buddhahood in this very body, it does not discuss the prior realization of holiness or the attainment of Buddhahood in a previous life; thus, he asked in this manner.

Now, since the Mahāyāna fully discusses both the fundamental and the phenomenal aspects, the Buddha’s response directly clarifies the matters of his birth in Tuṣita Heaven—both the primary and secondary retributions—as well as the practices of cultivation and non-cultivation, continuity and non-continuity, and so forth.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "One who has entered the stage of the Dharma-position receives the first prediction.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-saṃyojana-sūtra* states: "Maitreya has long since perfected his fundamental vows of compassion; therefore, he manifests as a Buddha."

The "Chapter on Dreaming Practice" (*Svapnāntaracaryā-parivarta*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Maitreya has long practiced the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), yet because he has nothing to be attained...

Furthermore, as stated in a volume of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: "In the past, within the city of Puṣpapura, he saw Dīpaṃkara Buddha and immediately attained [the realization of] the six *pāramitās*, even though he had not yet formally practiced them."
If that is so, can it be said that one does not cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or sever the afflictions (*kleśa*)?

The thirty-fourth fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The initial resolve and the ultimate goal are ultimately no different; of these two minds, the former is more difficult. To seek to save others before one has saved oneself—to such an initial resolve do I pay homage."

"Having resolved the mind [for enlightenment], one becomes a teacher of gods and humans, surpassing both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; such a resolution of the mind transcends the three realms, and for this reason it is called the supreme path."
The forty-seventh and forty-eighth fascicles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* state: "Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Sudhana:
'In this Jambudvīpa, within the southern region, in the country of Mālava, I was born into a Brahmin lineage in the village of Kuṭi.'"
In order to extinguish their prideful minds and to transform and deliver their parents and kinsmen, he takes birth among them;
having ended his life there, he is born in Tuṣita Heaven to transform and deliver them;
when his lifespan in that heavenly realm comes to an end, he descends to this world to achieve equal and perfect enlightenment.
You and Mañjuśrī both believe that you have seen me; therefore, go to Mañjuśrī’s place and inquire about the bodhisattva conduct and the cultivation of the bodhisattva path. Why is this?
“Mañjuśrī is always the mother of all Buddhas and always the teacher of all Bodhisattvas.
If this is so, and if various sutras clearly state this, can it be said that he does not cultivate meditative concentration and is without afflictions?

However, according to the tenets of the various masters, the stage of generating the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) is definitively placed below [the first bhūmi]; they provisionally designate the period prior to the definitive [attainment of] the stages as "generating the mind," which corresponds precisely to the level of a true ordinary person (pṛthagjana). It is for this reason that they make such a judgment.
Now, to clarify the stage of generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*), I shall explain it through the medium of provisional designations;
thus, they are indeed identical. Furthermore, upon examining various sutras, there are differing interpretations regarding the timing of the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni and Maitreya:
first, the various masters of the *Dicheng* (Earth-Collection) school state:
If Maitreya enters parinirvāṇa after people [have entered it], he must have been present at the time of Śākyamuni’s parinirvāṇa. How is this known?
For Maitreya was also there when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was preached.

If one reaches the Dharma assembly at the Twin Śāla Trees, the name of Maitreya will no longer appear in the list; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was preached at the end of the previous year, while the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* was preached at the beginning of this year. If Maitreya had been reborn in heaven after the Buddha’s passing, he would surely have been present at the Dharma assembly of the *Nirvāṇa*.
As for those who are not present now, you should know that they must have entered nirvana before the Buddha.
Second, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva Mipang refers generally to all bodhisattvas."
If that were so, Maitreya would be included within the category of the Bodhisattva Hongguang (Vipula), for there is no bodhisattva by the name of Hongguang.

Third, we now maintain that this is not the case. As the first group of masters states, and as the second group suggests there may be such a meaning, the first and hundredth fascicles of the *Śāstra* explicitly state: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Ānanda, Mañjuśrī, and Maitreya—these three persons compiled the Mahāyāna Piṭaka. Therefore, it is known that he entered nirvana only after the Buddha’s passing.
If that is so, because it is a summary, the name is not cited; alternatively, this may be as in the second explanation.
9. Distinguishing the Vehicles: Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The former masters say:
In Śākyamuni’s single dispensation, the manifestation of forms and the delivery of teachings do not exceed two paths:
First is worldly teaching;
second is world-transcending teaching.
Regarding the elucidation of worldly teaching, there are three types:
First is the three refuges;
second is the five precepts;
third is the ten wholesome actions.
Second, there are three types of supramundane teachings:
first, the Sudden Teaching, which is expounded for those of sharp faculties and great capacity, such as the *Avataṃsaka* and other Mahāyāna sūtras;
second, the Ad hoc and Indeterminate Teaching, which is for those of middling faculties, such as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* sūtras.
Third is the teaching of gradual progression; this is the expounding of sutras for those of inferior faculties, namely the teachings of the five periods, the four periods, and so forth.
Regarding this sutra, if one’s interpretation of the two kinds of supramundane Middle Way teachings is identical to that of the masters of the Three Teachings:

first, it is said that this is a specialized teaching (pianfang jiao) clarifying the causes and effects of the future, specifically the matters concerning the causes and effects of attaining Buddhahood in a Pure Land; both the primary and secondary fruits, as well as every detail of their sublime essence, are fully contained within the text of the sutra as explained.

Second, it is said that this is the sequential teaching; among the teachings of the five periods, this is the initial teaching. It explains the matter of attaining Buddhahood within a single lifetime alongside Śākyamuni, and it is also what is taught in the *Mūlamadhyama-sūtra* (or *Benmo jing*) as a small vehicle instruction on recorded events.

Furthermore, since this [text] has emerged from the Āgamas, and the Āgamas constitute the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, the principles contained in this scripture are therefore those of the Hīnayāna teachings.
If it were as separately explained in the *Mahāmaitrī-sūtra*, it would not necessarily have originated from within the *Āgamas*.

Furthermore, one source states that because this is a Mahāyāna teaching, the *Madhyama-āgama* also explains it as Mahāyāna; indeed, within the text of this very sūtra, there are expressions such as "permanence" (*nitya*) and "bliss" (*sukha*).

Now I say this is not so; since you claim that the *Āgama* sūtras are also Mahāyāna and the like, they are not the primary teaching, but rather the Mahāyāna is explained therein as a secondary exposition.

Therefore, it is now said that the *Sūtra on the Upper Rebirth* is the authentic and great teaching; thus, its text extensively elucidates the six perfections, the four immeasurables, the bodhisattva practices, and the unsurpassed path of the bodhicitta, as these are also fully discussed therein through the principle of provisional designation (*upāya*).
The third section, "Provisionally Clarifying the Tenets," explains that the *Mahāyāna* cause and effect are taught therein;
whereas the *Sūtra on the Descent [to Jambudvīpa]* takes the Hīnayāna as its tenet, and thus its text only attests to the four fruits of arhatship.
Question:
If that is so, why does the scriptural text speak of realizing the four virtues, such as permanence and bliss? Answer:

Terms such as "ordinary" and so forth are merely incidental; for instance, within the unconditioned state of *nirvāṇa* in the Hīnayāna, one may also figuratively record it as permanent and blissful, and in the Mahāyāna, the wondrous existence (*miao you*) can likewise clarify permanence and bliss. This may be analogized to the Mahāyāna.

As in the preceding examples from the Prajñā teachings, these may simply be cases of speaking of "permanence" and so forth in contrast to the realization of impermanence; why must they necessarily be directed at refuting the bhikṣus who cultivate the three [qualities] by asserting permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
10. The Tenth Section: Clarifying Miscellaneous Points of Distinction. Question:
Since this sutra is a Mahāyāna sutra, why does it not establish the five matters?
Answer: The tradition states that since this [text] was derived from the *Mahāsambodhi-sūtra*, it is thus abbreviated and does not establish the five matters.
The *Mahā-sūtra* says:
Since there are five matters [in the latter], the Small Version lacks them;
for example, the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* does not include these five matters, whereas the Large Version, the *Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood*, does include them.
The Buddha resided at Mount Śarabhaṅga (translated here as Guda Mountain) while traveling through the kingdom of Ujjayanta.
This was the place where past Buddhas had constantly subdued Māra; during the summer retreat, he walked up and down the mountain peak with Śāriputra and others, expounding the sutras to them.
Question:
The central tenet of this sutra is the cause and effect of the Pure Land; is this what is called the "substantial" Pure Land? Answer:
This land is a pure-impure land within the impure lands; it is not like the Pure Land of Amitāyus and others.
How is this known? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because it dwells upon the earth, it is not among the heavens;
because it is free from desire, it is not of the Desire Realm."

The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: "In the time when Maitreya appears in the world, women and others will still be practicing marriage at the age of five hundred; thus, one shall attain this excellent Pure Land."
Question:
For what reason did Śākyamuni leave home at nineteen and attain Buddhahood at thirty?
Why did Maitreya instead proceed to leave home and attain the Way during the first watch of the night?
Answer: It is said that because Maitreya has long since resolved his mind [on enlightenment], he attained the Way during the era of the Lesser Vehicle;
whereas because Śākyamuni’s resolve and attainment were more recent, he took a long time to attain the Way.
Question:

If it is because Śākyamuni’s resolve was formed recently that he has not yet attained Buddhahood—meaning that because his resolve was formed recently, he will attain Buddhahood later—why do you say that the former Buddha has already attained it?
Answer: Śākyamuni practiced diligence and asceticism; therefore, he attained Buddhahood first.
Question:

Regarding those who attained Buddhahood through diligent ascetic practices in previous lives: because they had already practiced such diligence and austerity, they were able to leave the household life and attain Buddhahood immediately; it should not be that they attained Buddhahood after a long period of time.

This is not necessarily so; it is clarified that [the Buddhas] manifest according to the capacities and circumstances of sentient beings, merely showing different expedient means over the long course of time.
A question is asked:
For what reason was Śākyamuni born into the Kṣatriya caste, while Maitreya was born into the Brāhmaṇa caste?
Answer:
Because the sentient beings transformed by Śākyamuni were stubborn and difficult to transform, he took birth in a noble clan to transform them.
Because the sentient beings to be transformed by Maitreya are gentle and easy to transform, he takes birth in a Brāhmaṇa family.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattva Womb Sūtra* (*Pusa chutai jing*) states: "For you who preach the Dharma, it is easy;
for me who preach the Dharma, it is difficult. The *Śāstra* (Treatise) says: "The Buddhas achieve the Way through eight phases:

first, ascending to heaven; second, descending into the womb; third, abiding in the womb; fourth, emerging from the womb; fifth, leaving home; sixth, attaining enlightenment; seventh, preaching the Dharma; and eighth, entering parinirvāṇa."
The *Mahāmaitrī-sūtra* states: "Seventh, begging for alms; eighth, seeking out Kāśyapa; ninth, entering parinirvāṇa. The *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* states:
"Riding upon the white elephant, he entered the place of the supreme sūtra; his body of birth remained in a celestial palace."
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* explains in detail the matter of entering the womb; it is extraordinary and inconceivable.

At the time when Maitreya Buddha appears in the world, one sowing will yield seven harvests; the rice will be seven inches long, white as jade or crystal, and as sweet as honey, just like the four-inch rice at the beginning of the kalpa.
The garments grow from trees, appearing spontaneously, just as they do in the northern continent of Uttarakuru.

Furthermore, the pearl pillars are long; according to the *Xiǎoběn* (Shorter Version), they are ten *lǐ* in height and illuminate an area of eight *yóujùn*, which is equivalent to three thousand two hundred *lǐ*.
Furthermore, it is called the "Bright Pearl Pillar" (*maṇi-stambha*); one interpretation says it is a pillar adorned with bright pearls, hence the term "bright pearl.
Another interpretation says the pillar itself is made of bright pearls, just as a pillar might be made of gold.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states that "the human lifespan was eighty-four thousand years.

Moreover, regarding the passage in a sūtra that speaks of "praising the body of skeletal remains," the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "Kāśyapa entered the samādhi of cessation; having attained the state of awaiting Maitreya’s appearance, and having ensured his three robes and alms bowl were complete, he did not enter the nirvāṇa of non-action."
